clinicalPearls: A perinatally lethal autosomal recessive osteochondrodysplasia caused by inactivating (loss-of-function) variants in PTH1R, the gene encoding the parathyroid hormone / parathyroid-hormone-related-peptide type 1 receptor.

The defining feature is markedly advanced skeletal maturation with dramatically accelerated endochondral ossification, the biological opposite of the receptor-activating Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia.
Presents with profound micromelia (severely shortened limbs), a hydropic fetus, increased bone density and short, dense long bones on prenatal or neonatal imaging.
Additional recognised features include facial dysmorphism, preauricular skin tags, dental abnormalities and, in some infants, aortic coarctation and abnormal cardiac or pulmonary development.

Because the same receptor mediates the actions of parathyroid hormone and PTH-related peptide, loss of signalling disrupts the PTHrP-Indian-hedgehog feedback loop that normally paces chondrocyte proliferation and delays their hypertrophic differentiation.
It is typically detected on second-trimester ultrasound or diagnosed at or shortly after birth; the condition is incompatible with survival.
Diagnosis is supported by characteristic radiographic and histological findings of accelerated, disorganised ossification and confirmed by biallelic PTH1R variant identification.
Genetic counselling for a one-in-four recurrence risk and the option of targeted prenatal or preimplantation testing in future pregnancies are central to management.
reference.pathophysiology: Blomstrand chondrodysplasia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in PTH1R, encoding the type 1 receptor shared by parathyroid hormone and parathyroid-hormone-related peptide (PTHrP). In the normal growth plate, PTHrP secreted at the ends of developing bones acts through this G-protein-coupled receptor on proliferating chondrocytes to keep them in the proliferative pool and delay their progression to terminal hypertrophic differentiation, forming a feedback circuit with Indian hedgehog that sets the pace of endochondral ossification. When receptor signalling is abolished, chondrocytes escape this restraint and differentiate and ossify prematurely, producing the hallmark of grossly advanced skeletal maturation with short, dense bones and a truncated proliferative zone. This mechanism stands in direct contrast to Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, in which activating variants of the same receptor cause constitutive signalling and delayed ossification; Blomstrand and Jansen thus represent the loss-of-function and gain-of-function poles of a single receptor disorder. Loss of the receptor also perturbs mineral handling and the development of teeth, breast and cardiovascular structures in which PTHrP signalling has a role.
additionalDifferentials: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (activating PTH1R variants, the mechanistic opposite)
Other lethal short-limb skeletal dysplasias such as thanatophoric dysplasia
Homozygous achondroplasia and severe FGFR3-related dysplasias
Eiken syndrome, a milder PTH1R-related skeletal disorder at the other end of the phenotypic range
additionalInvestigations: Detailed prenatal ultrasound documenting micromelia, hydrops and increased bone density
Fetal or neonatal skeletal survey radiography showing advanced, dense ossification
Histopathological examination of the growth plate demonstrating accelerated, disorganised endochondral ossification
Molecular testing for biallelic PTH1R variants in the affected fetus or neonate
Postmortem (perinatal autopsy) evaluation including cardiovascular and dental assessment
Parental carrier testing and, in later pregnancies, targeted prenatal diagnosis
redFlags: Second-trimester ultrasound showing severe micromelia with fetal hydrops
Radiographic evidence of grossly advanced ossification and dense short bones in a neonate
Associated aortic coarctation or other major cardiovascular malformation on prenatal imaging
Family history of a previous perinatally lethal short-limb skeletal dysplasia
reference.prognosis: Blomstrand chondrodysplasia is uniformly lethal in the perinatal period, with affected fetuses either stillborn or dying shortly after birth. Care is therefore directed at accurate diagnosis, compassionate perinatal support and genetic counselling regarding recurrence risk.
pitfalls: Confusing the loss-of-function Blomstrand phenotype with the activating Jansen disorder, which involves the same receptor but delayed ossification and postnatal survival.
Grouping it non-specifically with other lethal short-limb dysplasias and thereby missing the specific recurrence risk and testing options for the family.
Failing to arrange perinatal autopsy and molecular confirmation, which are essential for counselling.
Overlooking associated cardiovascular or dental anomalies that support the diagnosis.
Not recognising milder PTH1R-related conditions such as Eiken syndrome as part of the same allelic spectrum.
references: Standard reference atlas of constitutional disorders of bone (skeletal dysplasias)
Textbook of the metabolic and molecular bases of inherited disease
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, as the condition is uniformly lethal in the perinatal period, so care is palliative
Provide compassionate perinatal and end-of-life care for the affected neonate and family
Establish an accurate diagnosis with skeletal imaging and confirmatory biallelic PTH1R molecular testing
Offer perinatal autopsy to confirm the diagnosis and characterise associated cardiac and other anomalies
Provide genetic counselling regarding autosomal recessive inheritance and the recurrence risk to parents
Offer parental carrier testing and targeted prenatal diagnosis in future pregnancies
Provide bereavement support and involve clinical genetics and foetal medicine services
